title: Never enough thanks
hookLine: if our mouths were full of song as the sea, we still couldn't thank enough
carry: a mouth as full as the sea

cards: Have you ever tried to thank someone who saved you? A nurse who stayed through the night. A teacher who saw something in you.
A stranger who pulled over in the rain. You open your mouth and the words are too small. Thank you sounds like what you'd say for passing the salt.
On Shabbat and festival mornings, there's a prayer that starts from exactly that feeling, and doesn't try to hide it.

teach.h: THE BREATH OF EVERY LIVING THING.
teach.b: It's called Nishmat, from its first words, nishmat kol chai: the breath of every living thing shall bless your name.
It echoes the last line of the book of Psalms, in the old Jewish translation: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Hallelujah." Then comes its center.

teach.h: MOUTHS FULL OF SONG AS THE SEA.
teach.b: If our mouths were full of song as the sea, and our tongues full of joy like the roaring of its waves, and our lips full of praise like the wide sky, and our eyes shining like the sun and the moon, and our hands spread out like the eagles of heaven, and our feet as swift as deer, still we could not thank you enough for even one of the thousands upon thousands of kindnesses you have done for us and for our ancestors.
Read it slowly and you notice what it's doing.
It uses the whole body: mouth, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet. And it stretches each one to the size of the world: the sea, the sky, the sun. And then it admits defeat.
The thanks is in the admitting. Part of this language is old: the Talmud already quotes the line about mouths full of song as the sea, in a thanksgiving for rain.
Nishmat is said on Shabbat and festival mornings, and it's also sung at the Passover seder, near the end.
Many congregations mark it as a turning point in the Shabbat morning service: a new leader often steps up right around here. A thank-you that runs on and on, and then says it isn't long enough.

how: Nishmat is said in the Shabbat and festival morning service after the Song at the Sea, and in many congregations the leader for the main part of the service begins near its end; it is also recited at the Passover seder.

o: a Shabbat morning prayer: no thanks could ever be enough
a blessing said over wine as Shabbat begins
the silent standing prayer said three times a day

p: the breath of every living thing

s: Nishmat is said every weekday morning
it's said on Shabbat and festival mornings, and at the seder.
the line about mouths full of song as the sea appears in the Talmud
Nishmat ends by saying our thanks is enough
it says we could never thank enough for even one kindness.

games.q: you want to thank God with every part of yourself: mouth, eyes, hands, feet, stretched to the size of the sea and sky. where does Nishmat land?
o: still not enough for even one kindness.
games.why: not enough for even one of thousands upon thousands of kindnesses, and the admitting is the thanks.

practice: Think of the one person, or the one gift, you could never thank enough, and try to say thank you; notice how small the words are.
Then stop using words and let your breath be the thanks: each breath in, the gift; each breath out, the thanks you can't say.
